**Battle of Navarino**
The decisive 1827 naval battle of the Greek War of Independence, fought off the southwestern Peloponnese. An allied British, French, and Russian fleet under British admiral Edward Codrington destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet of Ibrahim Pasha, effectively securing Greek independence; Codrington was later criticized by the British Admiralty for provoking the engagement.

**Otto of Bavaria (Otto I)**
A Bavarian prince of the Wittelsbach dynasty who became the first king of modern Greece, installed by the Great Powers through the London Protocol and London Conference of 1832. He ruled from Athens (the capital was moved there from Nafplio), was forced to grant a constitution after the September 3rd Revolution of 1843, and was eventually deposed and exiled to Bavaria with his wife Amalia.

**Alexander Ypsilantis and the Filiki Eteria ("Society of Friends")**
The Filiki Eteria was a secret society that launched the Greek War of Independence in 1821. Its leader, Alexander Ypsilantis, was a Phanariote Greek and former Russian cavalry officer whose expedition into the Danubian Principalities was crushed at the Battle of Dragashani, after which he was imprisoned in Austria.

**Lord Byron and Missolonghi**
The English Romantic poet Lord Byron was a famous Philhellene who joined the Greek independence cause and died at Missolonghi in 1824. Missolonghi was later besieged and taken by Ibrahim Pasha, the son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt.

**Ibrahim Pasha**
The son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt, he led Egyptian forces on behalf of the Ottoman Sultan during the Greek War of Independence. He besieged Missolonghi and ravaged the Peloponnese, but his fleet was destroyed at Navarino.

**Regime of the Colonels**
The right-wing military junta that ruled Greece from 1967 to 1974 after a coup led by Georgios Papadopoulos. It was opposed by the student uprising at the Athens Polytechnic (National Technical University), which gave the name to the terrorist group Revolutionary Organization 17 November, and by the 1973 mutiny of the destroyer Velos during a NATO exercise; it collapsed after backing a coup against Archbishop Makarios III in Cyprus in pursuit of enosis.

**Greek Civil War and the Truman Doctrine**
A 1946 to 1949 civil war in which the communist Democratic Army of Greece (DSE) fought the royalist, US-backed government army. US support to Greece (and Turkey) under the 1947 Truman Doctrine was a key early Cold War policy; the war also saw children placed in "child towns" and refugee camps named for Queen Frederica.

**Massacre at Chios (Eugene Delacroix)**
An 1824 painting by the French Romantic artist Eugene Delacroix depicting the 1822 Ottoman slaughter and enslavement of Greek inhabitants of the island of Chios. It became a major symbol of the Greek cause in Western Europe.

**Greek debt crisis, PASOK, and SYRIZA**
After the government elected in 2009 revealed that its budget deficit was far higher than reported, Greece fell into a severe debt crisis requiring multiple EU bailout packages and raising fears of a "Grexit" from the Eurozone. Prime Minister George Papandreou of PASOK resigned, and in the January 2015 elections the leftist SYRIZA party won power under Alexis Tsipras, governing in coalition with the nationalist ANEL.

**Persian Wars (Marathon, Thermopylae, Salamis, Plataea)**
The early 5th-century BC conflicts in which Greek city-states such as Athens and Sparta repelled invasions by the Achaemenid Persian kings Darius I and Xerxes. Key battles include Marathon (490 BC), Thermopylae and Artemisium, the naval victory at Salamis led by Themistocles, and Plataea, where the Persian commander Mardonius was killed.

**Organization X and the December Events (Dekemvriana)**
Organization X was a right-wing royalist paramilitary group that fought the communist-led resistance movement EAM-ELAS. Their clash, along with British forces, in Athens in December 1944 is known as the December Events, a prelude to the Greek Civil War.

**Klephts and armatoloi**
Klephts were Greek mountain bandits who resisted Ottoman rule, while armatoloi were Christian militias employed by the Ottomans to keep order. Both groups became important fighters in the Greek War of Independence.

**Operation Mercury and the Metaxas Regime**
Greece under the "4th of August" dictatorship of Ioannis Metaxas resisted an Italian invasion in 1940 before being conquered by Germany in 1941. Operation Mercury was the German airborne invasion of Crete, the first major invasion conducted primarily by paratroopers, beginning with landings at Maleme airfield; Greece was then subjected to a "triple occupation" by Germany, Italy, and Bulgaria.

**Elgin Marbles and the Parthenon**
Marble sculptures removed from the Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens by Lord Elgin's agents between 1801 and 1812 and later sold to the British Museum. The Parthenon had earlier been badly damaged in 1687 when a Venetian bombardment ignited Ottoman gunpowder stored inside it.

**Mycenaeans and Linear B**
The Bronze Age civilization of mainland Greece known for Cyclopean masonry, the Lion Gate at Mycenae, and the Linear B script, an early form of Greek. The Mycenaeans supplanted the Minoan civilization centered at Knossos on Crete, and their collapse led to the Greek Dark Ages, which ended with the Geometric period.
